lead: A parse tree shows every grammar step, including nonterminals that carry no value. A syntax tree keeps only the operators and operands, so the expression's structure is easy to read. If the same subexpression appears twice, a syntax tree still stores it twice. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) stores it once and lets two parents point to the same node. Compilers build these forms before emitting intermediate code, because the DAG exposes repeated work that can be computed once. Some syllabi call this an expression DAG.
prereq: You need attributes from 4.1 and the parse-tree idea from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A parse tree for an expression has an interior node for every nonterminal used in the derivation. Many of those nodes are punctuation: they show which production was used, not which value is computed. A syntax tree removes them. Each interior node is an operator, and each leaf is an identifier or a constant. The children are the operands.

Build a syntax tree with two constructors. mkleaf(name) makes a leaf for a variable or constant. mknode(op, left, right) makes an operator node with a left child and a right child. For unary minus, use a node with one child. For a function call, the node holds the function name and its argument list.

For (a + b) * c, the root is *. Its left child is + with leaves a and b. Its right child is c. Parentheses do not appear as nodes; they only decide the shape. The syntax tree has 2 operator nodes and 3 leaves, so 5 nodes.
Semantic rules from 4.1 can return these nodes as synthesized attributes. The parser builds bottom-up: leaves first, then the operator above them.

Two occurrences of a + b in one expression compute the same value if a and b do not change between them. A DAG merges the two occurrences into one node. A DAG is a directed graph with no cycles. Leaves are variables or constants. Interior nodes are operators. An edge from a node to a child means "this operator uses that child". A node may be used more than once, and that is the whole point.

The value-number method builds the DAG in one pass. Give every distinct leaf a unique value number. For an operator node with operator op, left value number L and right value number R, look up the triple (op, L, R) in a table. If it exists, reuse that node. If not, create a node, give it the next value number, and record the triple. The value number is the node's identity. Equal numbers mean the same expression, so the compiler shares the node.

For (a + b) * (a + b) - c, the two plus nodes have the same triple (+, number of a, number of b). The second one is not created. The multiplication has the same plus node as both children. The DAG has 6 nodes instead of 9. The plus node is shared: the multiplication uses it as both children.

Sharing is common subexpression elimination at expression level. It saves evaluation time and storage. It is safe for pure arithmetic; with side effects or changing variables, the compiler must prove the value is unchanged.

A syntax tree and a DAG answer different questions. The syntax tree answers "how was this expression written?" The DAG answers "which values must be computed, and which results are reused?" Every DAG can be expanded into a syntax tree by copying a shared node once for each use. The reverse is also always possible: fold a syntax tree into a DAG by merging nodes that have the same operator and the same children. The fold saves nodes only when equal subtrees actually repeat.

Do not confuse this expression DAG with the basic-block DAG used in optimization. A basic-block DAG covers many statements and must respect assignments and side effects; that topic belongs to Unit 6. Here the DAG covers one expression.

The DAG is also a compact input to later stages. You can list its nodes in postfix order and emit three-address code from that list, or use the postfix list directly as stack-machine code. If a shared node is used several times, compute it once and let each use read the saved result.

spec.aria: Left, the syntax tree of (a + b) * (a + b) − c with two separate + subtrees; right, the DAG where both operands of * point to a single + node with leaves a and b.

examples.question: Draw the syntax tree and the DAG for (a + b) * (a + b) - c. Count the nodes, the node reduction, and the shared operator nodes.
steps: Find the outer operator. The root is -. Its left operand is (a + b) * (a + b) and its right operand is c.

Build the syntax tree. The multiplication has two children. The left child is + with leaves a and b. The right child is a second + with leaves a and b. The minus node has that multiplication on the left and c on the right.
Count syntax-tree nodes. Operators are -, *, +, +: 4 nodes. Leaves are a, b, a, b, c: 5 nodes. Total = 4 + 5 = 9 nodes.

Build the DAG. Leaves a and b get one node each. The first + creates a node for a + b. The second + has the same operator and the same child value numbers, so it reuses that node. The multiplication uses the same + node as both children. The minus node uses the multiplication and c.
Count DAG nodes. Operators are -, *, +: 3 nodes. Leaves are a, b, c: 3 nodes. Total = 3 + 3 = 6 nodes.
Count sharing. The plus node has two incoming edges, the left and right operands of the multiplication. Shared operator nodes = 1. Node reduction = 9 - 6 = 3 nodes.
examples.answer: Syntax tree: 9 nodes. DAG: 6 nodes. Reduction: 3 nodes. Shared operator nodes: 1.

traps: Do not merge a + b and b + a automatically. The triples (+, L, R) and (+, R, L) are different unless the compiler applies a commutative canonical order.

A DAG is not a syntax tree with missing labels. A shared node is used more than once (indegree ≥ 2); a syntax-tree node is used at most once (indegree ≤ 1). If no node in your drawing is used more than once (indegree ≤ 1 for every node), you drew a syntax tree.
Value numbers identify expressions within one pass. Two different variables can hold the same runtime value; the DAG must not share them just because their names look similar.
Do not count grammar nonterminals or parentheses in a syntax tree. Single-child chains from E to T to F are not nodes.
This expression DAG is not the basic-block DAG of Unit 6. Do not add assignment effects or statement order here.

quiz.q: What does a syntax tree keep from a parse tree?
quiz.a: It keeps operators and operands. It drops nonterminals and single-child punctuation nodes.

quiz.q: Why can a DAG node be used more than once?
quiz.a: Two occurrences of the same subexpression point to one shared node. The shared node then has one incoming edge for each use.

quiz.q: For (a * b) + (a * b), give the number of nodes in the syntax tree and in the DAG.
quiz.a: Syntax tree: operators +, *, * = 3; leaves a, b, a, b = 4; total 7. DAG: operators +, * = 2; leaves a, b = 2; total 4. The * node is shared.

quiz.q: A DAG has one operator node with indegree 3. What does this mean for evaluation?
quiz.a: The subexpression is used in three places (three edges enter the node, from one or more parents). Evaluate it once, store the result, and let all three uses read that saved result.

quiz.q: Name the two constructors used to build syntax-tree nodes.
In value numbering, what does the triple (op, L, R) mean?
quiz.a: It means operator op applied to a left subexpression with value number L and a right subexpression with value number R. If the triple already exists, reuse that node.

quiz.q: For a + (a + b), how many nodes are in the DAG?
quiz.a: Leaves a and b give 2 nodes. The inner plus gives 1 node. The outer plus gives 1 node. Total = 4 nodes. Leaf a is shared.

quiz.q: Can a DAG for an arithmetic expression contain a cycle? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Edges go from an operator to its operands, and operands are built before the operator. A cycle would make a node depend on itself, which a finite expression does not have.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production compilers use hash-consing to share equal subtrees and global value numbering to share equal values across basic blocks. Static single assignment (SSA) form gives each computed value one definition, which makes common subexpression elimination and constant propagation easier. E-graphs extend sharing to many equivalent expressions during optimization. Search for value numbering, hash-consing, SSA, and e-graphs.
